analysis.one_liner: Forces factories and chemical plants to sharply cut toxic air emissions and prevent chemical accidents.
analysis.headline: This toxic air pollution bill drew 93 bipartisan cosponsors and held hearings, but never got a committee vote; its substance instead became part of the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the Clean Air Act's rules on toxic air pollution. It lists more than 180 hazardous chemicals, orders the EPA to set strict emission standards for industrial categories of polluters within eight years, requires polluters to get five-year operating permits, and makes them install leak-detection and run annual safety inspections. It bans the sale of leaded gasoline, sets diesel soot limits for cars, trucks, and buses, and requires chemical facilities to write risk-management plans to prevent catastrophic accidental releases, with an independent board to investigate major chemical accidents.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near industrial facilities and in large cities, where toxic air pollutants like benzene, formaldehyde, mercury, and diesel soot concentrate. Workers at chemical plants gain from mandatory safety inspections, leak detection, and accident-prevention plans. Children and city residents gain from the leaded-gasoline ban and diesel particulate limits.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs EPA to set emission standards for every category of major industrial polluter within eight years, requiring the best available control technology, with a standard imposed automatically by law if EPA misses a deadline [S2][S3].

Major emitting facilities must obtain five-year permits, pay annual fees, monitor emissions, allow public comment on permits, and pass facility inspections, and all permit records are made public [S2][S3].
It bans sale of leaded gasoline for motor vehicles by 1991 at the latest and sets diesel particulate standards for passenger vehicles, trucks, and buses starting in model years 1991-1992 [S2][S3].

Chemical facilities must list dangerous substances, prepare risk-management plans for preventing and responding to accidental releases, and submit to an independent Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board that investigates accidents and makes its findings public [S2][S3].

Residents of large metropolitan areas gain from mandatory monitoring of toxic air pollutants and an urban air toxics research program, and the EPA must identify metropolitan areas facing the highest risks and name their sources [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Chemical manufacturers, oil refiners, and other industrial operators bear the cost of emission controls, permits, fees, monitoring, inspections, and accident-prevention programs. Diesel engine and vehicle makers and gasoline sellers face new fuel and vehicle standards. Some of these compliance costs would be passed to consumers in the prices of goods and fuel.

drawbacks.text: The bill takes costs into account in setting standards, but strict best-available-technology requirements for existing plants can be expensive, and those costs would partly show up in consumer prices and could pressure marginal facilities and jobs [S3].

The bill includes substantial carve-outs: the President can exempt facilities for national security reasons in two-year renewable increments, existing facilities can receive up to three two-year compliance extensions, and facilities that cut emissions 95 percent early can be exempted from standards entirely [S2][S3].

States can take over permitting and enforcement, and while EPA must review state programs every two years and can withdraw approval, day-to-day enforcement would depend heavily on state capacity [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets pollutants with well-documented health harms — carcinogens like benzene and vinyl chloride, metals like mercury and lead, diesel soot — and its permit, monitoring, and public-disclosure requirements give communities real information about what is in their air. The main honest objection is cost: retrofitting existing plants is expensive, and the bill spreads the burden across industry rather than directing aid to workers or communities hit by plant closures. The compliance deadlines are long (three to eight years) and the exemptions generous, which softens the cost but also delays the benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, held a subcommittee hearing, and gathered 93 cosponsors, but was never reported out of committee; the final action entry simply points to H.R. 3030, the vehicle that became the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990.

narrative.text: Rep. Mickey Leland of Texas introduced the bill on June 8, 1989, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1][S5].
The bill drew 93 cosponsors — 72 of 257 House Democrats and 21 of 175 House Republicans — and initial sponsors included members of both parties [S3][S4].
The Subcommittee on Health and the Environment held hearings on June 22, 1989, and the bill was referred to that subcommittee [S5].
The bill never received a markup or a vote; after additional cosponsors were added in May 1990, the action history states 'For Further Action See H.R.3030' [S5].

The substance of the bill — an air toxics program, accidental-release prevention, and a chemical safety investigation board — closely matches the toxic air pollutant and chemical safety provisions Congress enacted in the Clean Air Act Amendments later that session of Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the end, the public largely won: a version of this air toxics program, the leaded-gasoline phase-out, and the chemical accident provisions became law in the Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990. What the bill's operators avoided was this specific, stricter design and its earlier deadlines — the enacted program gave industrial facilities a different standard-setting structure and more lead time.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industry got a slower, revised program

for.name: Rep. Mickey Leland
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Air Toxics Control Act of 1989 and organized an initial bipartisan group of co-sponsors.

for.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
for.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Health and the Environment (D-CA)
for.what_they_did: Held a subcommittee hearing on the bill in June 1989 and later submitted additional cosponsors on its behalf.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee and never reported it out; no markup or floor vote ever occurred in the 101st Congress.

against.name: Chemical, refining, and auto-diesel industries
against.what_they_did: Faced comprehensive emission standards, permit fees, and accident-prevention requirements under the bill; their opposition to strong air toxics controls was widely reported during the 1989-1990 clean air debate.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship crossed party lines — 72 of 257 House Democrats and 21 of 175 House Republicans signed on — and the bill never reached a vote that would have tested partisan divisions.

industries.note: The bill lists over 180 hazardous chemicals, requires best-available-technology emission standards, five-year permits with fees, leak-detection and annual safety inspections, and risk-management plans for accidental releases, plus an independent board investigating chemical accidents. These are direct costs to an industry whose emissions expose nearby residents and plant workers.
The bill bans the sale of leaded gasoline for motor vehicles by January 1, 1991 at the latest, ending a product whose lead emissions poison children and city residents.

industries.industry: Diesel engine and commercial vehicle makers
industries.note: The bill sets diesel particulate standards for passenger vehicles from model year 1992, heavy trucks from 1991-1994, and buses, and requires retrofit controls on existing diesel buses — costs that reduce urban diesel soot exposure.

industries.industry: State and local air pollution agencies
industries.note: The bill authorizes federal grants, requires toxic air monitoring in large metropolitan areas, and lets states take over permitting and enforcement with federal funding — building public-sector capacity to protect air quality.
